# finite-state-machine-ts

Readable finite state machines for TypeScript using decorators and normal class methods.

This file is a compact guide for AI coding assistants and other tools that need to use `finite-state-machine-ts` correctly.

> Repository contributors: see AGENTS.md for repository and development guidance.

## Core rules

- Use string-valued states only.
- Subclass `StateMachine<S extends string>`.
- Set `static initialState` for new machine instances, or pass an explicit state to the constructor when restoring persisted state.
- Put transition behavior on decorated methods with `@transition(...)`.
- Use `source`, `target`, optional `conditions`, and optional `onError` to describe allowed state changes.
- Use `generateStateDiagram(...)` or `fsm-draw-state-diagram` to derive Mermaid diagrams from declared transitions.
- Do not expect a separate central machine configuration API. The methods are the machine.

## Canonical state definition

Prefer an `as const` object when you want named values:

```ts
const JobState = {
  Queued: "queued",
  Running: "running",
  Completed: "completed",
  Failed: "failed",
} as const;

type JobState = (typeof JobState)[keyof typeof JobState];
```

String unions and string enums also work, but state values must be strings.

## Canonical usage

```ts
import { StateMachine, transition } from "finite-state-machine-ts";

const JobState = {
  Queued: "queued",
  Running: "running",
  Completed: "completed",
  Failed: "failed",
} as const;

type JobState = (typeof JobState)[keyof typeof JobState];

class BackgroundJob extends StateMachine<JobState> {
  static initialState: JobState = JobState.Queued;
  shouldFail = false;

  @transition<JobState, BackgroundJob, [], void>({
    source: JobState.Queued,
    target: JobState.Running,
  })
  start() {}

  @transition<JobState, BackgroundJob, [], void>({
    source: JobState.Running,
    target: JobState.Completed,
    onError: JobState.Failed,
  })
  process() {
    if (this.shouldFail) {
      throw new Error("job failed");
    }
  }
}

const freshJob = new BackgroundJob();
const restoredJob = new BackgroundJob(JobState.Failed);

freshJob.start();
```

## Conditions and async transitions

Conditions receive the machine instance and can return `boolean` or `Promise<boolean>`.

```ts
import { StateMachine, transition } from "finite-state-machine-ts";

class Deployment extends StateMachine<"pending" | "running"> {
  static initialState: "pending" | "running" = "pending";

  @transition<"pending" | "running", Deployment, [], Promise<void>>({
    source: "pending",
    target: "running",
    conditions: [async () => true],
  })
  async start() {
    await Promise.resolve();
  }
}
```

Async transitions do not update `state` until the async work finishes.

## Diagram generation

Programmatic usage:

```ts
import { generateStateDiagram } from "finite-state-machine-ts";

const diagram = generateStateDiagram(BackgroundJob, {
  initialState: JobState.Queued,
});
```

CLI usage after building the package:

```bash
fsm-draw-state-diagram --class ./dist/path/to/machine.js:BackgroundJob --initial-state queued
```

The `--class` argument format is `<module-path>:<export-name>`.

## Common mistakes to avoid

- Do not forget `"experimentalDecorators": true` in `tsconfig.json`.
- Do not use number, symbol, or object state values.
- Do not assume async transitions update `state` before the promise resolves.
- Do not mutate `state` manually during normal transitions; use decorated methods. Passing a constructor state for restore/init flows is fine.
- Do not expect a central machine config object or statechart DSL in this library.
